From shops across the Causeway to storefronts in China, PayLah! users can scan to pay just as they do at Singapore’s hawker centres – where PayLah! accounts for more than 60 per cent of QR transactions.

“The way people pay has evolved significantly over the past decade, and so have their expectations. Today, customers value not just the ability to pay digitally, but how simple and seamless the experience is,” said Chan Sow Han, head of Payments and Unsecured Lending at DBS Singapore.

“Our focus is to build on what customers already know and use, extending that ease of payment across more situations and locations so they can use PayLah! to pay wherever they are, while continuing to enhance the experience to better serve their needs.”

Making payments anywhere

QR payments are widely used across Asia, but payment systems and practices differ across markets. In China, for instance, customers may scan a merchant’s QR code or present their own for the cashier to scan.

DBS is addressing this through its latest expansion of PayLah!, which enables users to make QR payments at over 100 million participating Alipay+ and Weixin Pay merchants across China.

On top of existing UnionPay QR connectivity, DBS is the first and only bank in Singapore to support both payment methods across China’s three major QR payment ecosystems.

The development marks another milestone in DBS’ efforts to extend the payment habits Singaporeans are accustomed to at home across international borders. According to DBS, in 2022, it became the first bank in Singapore to enable consumers to make QR payments globally using a local app, through its partnership with UnionPay International.

Since then, PayLah!’s overseas reach has grown through partnerships with payment networks. These include DuitNow in Malaysia, PromptPay in Thailand and QRIS in Indonesia, allowing customers to scan to pay when travelling to these destinations. This year, DBS said it also became the first Singapore bank to connect to Taiwan’s TWQR network, allowing PayLah! users to scan to pay at over 250,000 participating merchants in Taiwan.

“While QR payments are increasingly common across Asia, different markets have their own payment systems and ways of transacting. Our approach has been to work with established payment networks and partners to bridge these differences, so customers can enjoy a more consistent payment experience when travelling,” said Chan.

These efforts have translated into growing customer usage. Last year, PayLah!’s cross-border QR transaction volumes have grown 2.5 times year-on-year, while the number of unique users has doubled. Average spending per customer on PayLah!’s overseas QR transactions has also increased by approximately 30 per cent in the same period.

Recognising that customers have different payment preferences when travelling, DBS also introduced the TravelLah! Debit Card in September 2026, complementing PayLah!’s overseas QR payment capabilities with a debit card option.

Available to customers aged 16 and above, TravelLah! offers zero foreign exchange fees, using Visa exchange rates without additional mark-ups from DBS. Customers can pay in more than 150 currencies worldwide and view indicative exchange rates directly on the PayLah! app, giving them greater visibility over prevailing rates before they spend.

TravelLah! also offers zero DBS fees on overseas ATM withdrawals, with no cap on the amount or frequency of overseas withdrawals.

The accompanying TravelLah! Debit Card Wallet within DBS PayLah! held in Singapore dollars can be topped up as needed, allowing customers to set aside funds for their travels without having to pre-convert or manage multiple currencies. Cardholders can also redeem complimentary basic travel insurance, subject to terms and conditions.

The card has attracted interest among younger customers, with around half of those who signed up in its first month aged between 16 and 29.

Designed for every stage of life

Beyond expanding where and how customers can pay, DBS is also enhancing PayLah! to better serve the needs of different customer groups.

“With a user base spanning different generations and life stages, we recognise that what customers expect from a payment app can vary considerably,” Chan explains. “A teenager learning to manage an allowance has different needs from a young adult travelling overseas or a senior who values simplicity when making digital payments.”

Rather than offering the same experience to everyone, DBS is moving towards a more personalised PayLah! experience, where customers can more easily access the features, offers and rewards most relevant to them.

For younger customers, DBS PayLah! for Teens, introduced in April 2026, offers an age-appropriate payment experience, including the ability to receive allowances digitally, customise transfer limits, and access relevant coupons and rewards. It also comes with built-in safeguards, including disabled auto-debit and spending controls, to help teenagers gain confidence in making digital payments safely.

A new senior-friendly mode was also launched last month, offering a simpler setup, with larger text, clearer navigation and easy access to core payment functions.

PayLah! also makes it easier for customers to get more value from their everyday spending. Those with DBS/POSB cards that earn DBS Points or POSB Daily$ can use their points to redeem a wide variety of rewards, including instantly offsetting eligible transactions, exchanging points for cash credits or Flexi eVouchers which can be used at NETS merchants across Singapore.

Beyond tailoring the experience to different users, DBS has also simplified everyday payment journeys, including online shopping through PayLah! Express Checkout. The feature enables customers to link their account once and subsequently complete purchases on participating platforms such as Lazada, foodpanda and Gojek. This allows customers to pay without switching between apps or entering card details on individual platforms.

Greater control and peace of mind

Backed by DBS, PayLah! combines the convenience of an everyday wallet with safeguards and customer controls that help customers manage their spending and transact with greater confidence.

To further safeguard customers, DBS will soon introduce complimentary wallet protection for all PayLah! users, providing coverage against unauthorised third-party transactions.

Looking ahead, DBS will continue expanding PayLah!’s payment capabilities while making the experience more personalised and rewarding.

“As we expand PayLah!’s capabilities, our focus is not simply on adding more features, but on making the experience more relevant to customers’ needs. We want them to derive greater value from each interaction, while retaining the simplicity and convenience they value,” said Chan.

data.title: After US$6.3 billion crypto heist, Binance plans foray into 5 Asian markets
data.description:
SINGAPORE – Binance, the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, plans to expand into five Asian markets in 2027 with South and South-east Asia as key priorities, its regional business head said, not long after the firm was hit with a record US$6.3 billion (S$8.1 billion) digital heist in October.

“We have ongoing conversations with at least five or six markets... three of which are in quite mature stages,” S.B. Seker told Reuters on the sidelines of the Singapore FinTech Festival on Nov 18. “The others are ongoing conversations.”

He did not specify the new markets that Binance, which currently has operating licences in more than 10 jurisdictions, was looking at, but said details of the planned expansion were expected to be rolled out in the first quarter of 2027.

Binance’s expansion plans come on the heels of a security breach linked to North Korea that resulted in US$6.3 billion being stolen from its platform in October.

The Federal Bureau of Investigation and Binance have said North Korea was responsible for the hack, but Pyongyang has denied that.

The company, which resumed withdrawals in phases earlier in November after covering 95% of the lost tokens, said last weekend it aimed to reopen withdrawals for all remaining networks and assets by the end of this week.

The Binance heist, which has been described by experts as the largest crypto theft ever, has renewed scrutiny of inconsistent security practices in the industry.

Seker, the firm’s head of APAC, said Binance contacted a number of regulators, including those in Japan, South Korea, Australia, Thailand and New Zealand, within the first 36 to 48 hours of the incident, to address questions about the scale of its impact and how the attack unfolded.

“Think of all the financial services regulators and markets where we are present,” he said, adding that there was no one country that led the charge in the investigations.

Binance says the Abu Dhabi Global Market’s Financial Services Regulatory Authority is its primary regulator.

Seker said that while discussions with regulators were ongoing, the conversation had moved beyond the heist to broader concerns about security threats facing the crypto industry.

“The conversations now are ‘Well, this is an omnipresent and spectrum-wide threat, and how does an entire ecosystem prepare for this?’ It’s moved away from the original incident to a much broader conversation,” he said.

“We are part of the conversation, but we are not driving the conversation in isolation anymore.” REUTERS

data.title: UN says Singapore’s Penguin International broke Libya arms embargo; company disputes panel’s findings
data.description:
SINGAPORE - Singapore-listed shipbuilder Penguin International has disputed a United Nations panel’s finding that its sale of two vessels subsequently shipped to Libya violated an arms embargo, saying the vessels were built for commercial use and delivered without weapons.

In a bourse filing on Nov 17, the company said the transaction involved a security vessel and a landing craft sold in December 2024 to Dubai-based 2020 Volume Boats.

Both vessels were delivered from Penguin’s yard in Singapore, and then shipped to Benghazi, Libya.

On Mar 24, 2026, the UN Panel of Experts on Libya published a report naming Penguin and its wholly owned subsidiary, Penguin Shipyard Asia.

The panel classified the security vessel as a naval-type fast patrol vessel and the landing craft as a dual-use vessel, and considered their transfer to Libya a violation of an arms embargo imposed under UN Security Council Resolution 1970.

However, the panel did not recommend sanctions against Penguin or its subsidiary.

Penguin said it disagreed with the panel’s characterisation of the vessels and its conclusion that the transaction breached the arms embargo.

The company maintained that both vessels had been designed and built for commercial purposes and were delivered without arms or ammunition on board.

Penguin said it had corresponded with the UN panel between January and May in 2025 and provided the information requested in relation to the transaction.

It became aware of the panel’s report in September 2026, about six months after its publication, and subsequently engaged Singapore legal counsel and an international sanctions specialist to assess the implications.

Based on the advice received, Penguin said being named in the report did not itself constitute a sanctions action or impose any direct penalties.

The company also understood that the likelihood of the UN imposing sanctions against Penguin or its subsidiary on the basis of the report was low.

Separately, Penguin has been corresponding with Singapore Customs since November 2025 regarding the export of the vessels.

The company said the matter had not materially disrupted its operations, and its board was not presently aware of any material financial impact. THE BUSINESS TIMES

data.title: Anthropic pulled off the biggest IPO ever. What that means, by the numbers
data.description:
Anthropic has made a superlative-filled debut on Wall Street, breaking all records for money raised on Wall Street as it became the first major artificial intelligence lab to become a publicly traded company.

The price tag on its shares was enough to put the value of the San Francisco company well beyond US$1 trillion (S$1.29 trillion).

That kind of number was once unheard of for a company’s first moments trading on the stock market. But an acceleration in corporate wealth – and most recently the AI boom – has changed that.

Anthropic is the second business to debut with a value over a trillion dollars, following SpaceX just months ago, and will join a handful of other tech giants that measure their wealth by figures reaching 13 digits.

Time will tell how Anthropic ultimately fares on the public market. The Claude maker decided to proceed with its IPO despite jitters among some investors over market volatility, fears of a possible AI bubble and growing unease among the public about the technology’s risks overall.

Here are some numbers to help understand the IPO on Nov 19.

The amount in proceeds raised by the offering: US$81 billion

That makes Anthropic’s debut the biggest ever. Ahead of trading on Nov 19, it offered 980 million shares priced at US$83 each, putting Anthropic ahead of Elon Musk’s SpaceX, which set a previous record with its IPO proceeds of about US$75 billion in June.

The next biggest IPO hauls went to South Korean chipmaker SK Hynix US$26.5 billion in July and oil giant Saudi Aramco US$25.6 billion in 2019.

Anthropic’s initial valuation: US$1.5 trillion

The initial price per share was set at US$83. But that spiked more than 30% to open at US$111.50 a share – pushing the company’s total valuation by half a trillion dollars to US$2.01 trillion just before noon Eastern time (1am Singapore time on Nov 20).

By market close on Nov 19, Anthropic finished its first trading day at US$97.17 per share. That is still over 17% higher than its initial public offering price, and amounts to a market value of roughly US$1.75 trillion.

In June, SpaceX ended its first day of trading on the public market with a valuation of US$2.1 trillion. Its market cap has since fallen to closer to US$1.95 trillion.

Number of public companies that have reached the trillion-dollar club in the S&P 500: 11

Apple currently leads the pack at US$5.1 trillion, followed by Microsoft (US$3.8 trillion) and Nvidia (US$3.6 trillion), among others. That does not count SpaceX and Anthropic, which also have joined the trillion-dollar club even though they are not in the S&P 500 index yet.

Only in recent memory have major corporations been valued over US$1 trillion. iPhone maker Apple was the first to pass that threshold, back in 2018.

How far a trillion US dollar bills would stretch if laid end to end: 156 million kilometres

That would surpass the roughly 150 million kilometres between Earth and the sun.

The number “one trillion” is hard in itself for the human mind to comprehend. US$1 trillion is a thousand times greater than US$1 billion. And a million times more than US$1 million.

There are more than 8.2 billion people living on Earth today, per the US Census Bureau. If US$1 trillion was divided among the entire population, each person would receive almost US$122. AP

data.title: GTA VI promises Sony a windfall, but Japan plays by different rules
data.description:
TOKYO – The global launch of Grand Theft Auto VI on Nov 19 is expected to provide a major boost to PlayStation maker Sony, though the franchise remains a niche pursuit in its home market of Japan.

The long-awaited, open-world, crime action game from Take-Two Interactive’s Rockstar Games is rolling out across the world, and has been met with rave reviews and fans taking time off work to play.

About three-quarters of the 17 million GTA VI units sold are on PlayStation, according to estimates from Sensor Tower, outselling Xbox maker Microsoft.

Shares in Sony, whose PlayStation 5 (PS5) console is in its seventh year on the market, were up almost 3% in Tokyo compared with flat trading in the benchmark index.

Analysts think the global enthusiasm is unlikely to reach a fever pitch in Japan, where Switch 2 maker Nintendo dominates the gaming device market, and consumers prefer anime-style titles to realistic, violent Western games.

“The current trends in Japan don’t really fit this kind of game,” said Toyo Securities analyst Hideki Yasuda.

Given worldwide demand, “there’s absolutely no need for this game to sell in Japan”, he said.

Earlier in 2026, Sony scored a major global success with the movie Spider-Man: Brand New Day. In Japan, however, it faced competition from breakout hit Chiikawa The Movie: The Secret Of Mermaid Island.

“A few of my friends bought GTA VI at midnight, but I’m in no hurry to as it’s only on PS5 and Xbox, and you can’t play multiplayer online yet,” said Sorataka Goto, 33, who was shopping in Tokyo’s Akihabara electronics district.

“If and when it’s on PC and you can play online, I’ll consider buying it,” added Goto, who bought the remake of The Legend Of Zelda: Ocarina Of Time.

Nintendo has sold more than five million copies of the Switch 2 title, which was originally on the Nintendo 64, in the first four days since its launch earlier in November.

“I had the original as a child, and so was excited to try this version,” Goto said.

GTA VI hype reaches Japan

Gamers in Japan may struggle to fully understand the satirical elements of GTA VI, the references to the Florida lifestyle and Western memes, said Serkan Toto, founder of game industry consultancy Kantan Games.

Still, the worldwide hype for GTA VI is spilling over to Japan, and marketing in the country is unprecedented for a Western-made game, he said.

In Akihabara, a large poster featuring the lead characters, Lucia Caminos ​and Jason Duval, was plastered on the side of a building.

“GTA VI will not become a mega blockbuster in Japan, but it will do very, very well,” Toto said.

Analysts expect the release of GTA VI to soften the decline of PS5 hardware sales in 2026 and support growth in software sales.

Sony sold 2.6 million PS5 units during the July-September quarter, which analysts see as reflecting demand ahead of GTA VI, down from 4 million a year earlier.

“We’ve modelled PlayStation profits materially ahead of the Street in the next couple of quarters, on account of the GTA VI launch,” Bernstein analyst David Dai wrote in a note.

The release is bolstering Sony’s games slate after it delayed the launch of God Of War Laufey by three months to May 2027.

Sony is grappling with procurement challenges as the cost of memory chips has risen sharply due to the AI boom.

“I don’t get the sense that Sony has much desire to aggressively sell hardware. The benefits Sony gets from royalties will be enormous,” said Toyo Securities’ Yasuda. REUTERS

data.title: MindChamps founder seeks $86m for first pre-school fund to expand in Australia
data.description:
The founder of Singapore-listed MindChamps PreSchool has launched an investment platform that is seeking to raise A$100 million (S$86.4 million) for its first fund to acquire and develop purpose-built pre-school properties in Australia.

The platform, MindFunds, will pursue investments across the education sector, David Chiem, founder of MindChamps, a franchiser of pre-school centres, said in an interview.

The company has sold 45 franchise licences as part of its expansion in Australia, and the fund will acquire or develop properties where franchisees can open and operate their centres, he said.

MindChamps is targeting a first close for the fund in the first half of 2027, according to Goh Seh Harn, chief executive officer of Trigger Asset Management, who advises on the fund. It also plans a follow-on fund of A$500 million, he said.

Across Asia, growing demand for quality education has fuelled a rush of private capital into schools, opening up new sources of funding for a sector that has traditionally relied on equity and bank loans. Financiers such as Apollo Global Management and KKR & Co have bought stakes and lent money to school chains, betting that rising incomes and families’ willingness to spend more on their children will spur expansion.

MindChamps operates pre-schools, after-school care centres and therapy services for children. The Singapore-based company has also expanded into markets including Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines and Myanmar. BLOOMBERG

data.title: UOB to use A*STAR’s multilingual AI tool to guide S-E Asia relationship managers on client calls
data.description:
SINGAPORE – UOB and A*STAR have tied up to explore how an artificial intelligence tool can help relationship managers better engage clients, as the bank drives greater deployment of AI across its operations.

The tool is designed to transcribe and translate customer calls in real time, and prompt relationship managers with questions to ask and disclosures to make so they comply with regulatory guidelines.

Built on A*STAR’s large language model MERaLiON, the AI solution can understand 11 languages and dialects spoken in South-east Asia, where UOB’s retail customers are concentrated.

“(We) see potential for this solution to help our relationship managers better understand customers, navigate language and cultural nuances, and provide clearer, more relevant guidance,” said UOB’s group chief financial officer Leong Yung Chee in a statement on Nov 18 on the first day of the Singapore FinTech Festival.

In a demonstration to the media on Nov 13, UOB and A*STAR showed a mock customer call in which an early version of the tool could log sentences spoken in a mix of English, Mandarin and Malay.

When the relationship manager neglected to properly verify the client’s identity, the tool flagged it in red, prompted her to ask for an NRIC number and suggested a scripted line.

Panchai Aroonpairoj, a senior client adviser at UOB Private Bank, said the tool could come in handy when he speaks with older Thai clients, who may sometimes use Teochew phrases during their calls.

As he does not understand the dialect, he would otherwise have to ask them to repeat themselves in Thai, disrupting the flow of the conversation.

UOB believes that the solution could also provide insights for more targeted coaching of relationship managers, complementing existing training methods such as role-playing while a human observer gives feedback.

The bank hopes to roll out the AI tool some time in 2027, though there is no fixed timeline yet, said UOB’s head of enterprise AI Alvin Eng.

For now, A*STAR and UOB will work on developing the application and tailoring it to the bank’s needs.

Angela Chee, a director at A*STAR’s Institute of Advanced Intelligence and Computing, said this would mark MERaLiON’s first use case in the banking sector.

Other banks such as DBS, OCBC and Standard Chartered have also been testing the model and evaluating how they would use it.

The model’s existing users include social service agency Lions Befrienders, which has a MERaLiON-powered voice agent to automate check-in calls on seniors, and tech service provider NCS, which uses the model for voice transcription for its in-house chatbot.

“A large part of our work will be doing model adaptation to see how we can teach the model to speak or to think like a financial person, so (it) can transcribe more accurately,” said Chee.

A*STAR will have to familiarise MERaLiON with the terminology and acronyms that UOB uses, and incorporate feedback from the bank as it tests the solution.

UOB, like many banks, has been stepping up its deployment of AI to streamline workflows and drive value. It has more than 300 AI and data analytics use cases, including a solution that optimises cash replenishment routes and schedules for its ATMs.

The MERaLiON solution will not supplant its relationship managers. “That’s not our philosophy,” said Eng, adding that the tool is meant to augment staff.

For Aroonpairoj, the value of his team is clear. “You need relationships, which means you need human touch,” he said. “People will trust humans more than machines.”

data.title: Anthropic’s IPO: Will Singapore investors back AI’s promise or help fuel another bubble?
data.description:
SINGAPORE – Anthropic’s upcoming listing will put the market’s appetite for artificial intelligence to the test.

Do investors still see AI as a lucrative opportunity? Or have concerns over lofty valuations, soaring spending and uncertain returns brought them back down to earth?

The Nov 19 Nasdaq listing of the company behind the Claude chatbot comes amid significant volatility in AI-related stocks.

Anthropic is seeking a valuation of up to US$1.4 trillion (S$1.8 trillion), according to its latest initial public offering (IPO) plans. It is offering 825 million shares at between US$70 and US$78 apiece, potentially raising US$64.4 billion, including shares sold by existing shareholders, which could make it the biggest IPO in history.

A strong debut would signal that investors still see fortunes to be made from AI.

Conversely, a lacklustre one might suggest that investors are becoming more discerning about the prices they are prepared to pay for the stock.

A subsequent fall in Anthropic’s share price could signal either a broader loss of confidence in AI or a reassessment of the company’s valuation and prospects.

This does not have to be a bad thing, though. Given the transformational potential and benefits of AI, a correction could be an opportunity for more sensible, long-term value investors to enter the market.

Promise and peril

Founded in 2021, the San Francisco-based company develops the Claude family of AI models used for tasks ranging from writing and software development to research and data analysis.

Anthropic plans to use the proceeds from the offering and a concurrent US$26 billion private placement to fund general corporate purposes, including investments in computing infrastructure, research and development, and business expansion.

Its prospectus points to the technology’s potential to accelerate scientific discoveries, help researchers tackle diseases such as cancer and improve productivity across both the public and private sectors.

In healthcare, for example, AI could help doctors identify diseases earlier and aid researchers in developing new treatments. In education, it could provide personalised learning support, while businesses could use it to improve efficiency and reduce costs.

The strategic and national importance of AI is also evident in the lengths to which the US has gone to restrict China’s access to advanced semiconductors.

On Nov 16, Washington announced new restrictions requiring US export licences for shipments of certain advanced AI chips to data centres in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand and Indonesia, among other countries, as it seeks to prevent Chinese companies from accessing American computing power through overseas facilities.

The rule underscores the urgency with which the Commerce Department is scrambling to crack down on Chinese access to sensitive American technology, following reporting that the agency turned a blind eye to smuggling of advanced Nvidia chips to China.

But Anthropic’s prospectus also lays bare the formidable costs and risks of developing the technology.

The company further warned that sufficiently advanced AI systems could pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity if developed or deployed without adequate safeguards.

Such risks could arise if AI systems were weaponised, misused or allowed to operate with a high degree of autonomy, particularly if advances in the technology outpace developers’ ability to evaluate and control them.

The prospectus also highlights the possibility that increasingly autonomous systems could take harmful actions without human intervention.

Meanwhile, the company is still unprofitable, recording a net loss of US$104 billion for the first nine months of the year, compared with US$25.1 billion in the same period in 2025.

Anthropic has also disclosed approximately US$900.9 billion in purchase and lease commitments, much of it related to computing capacity and infrastructure extending over many years.

These levels of expenditure raise questions about whether the company can sustain its growth, maintain its technological advantage and generate sufficient profits to justify investors’ expectations.

Lessons from past bubbles

But even a strong debut could prompt questions about whether speculation is running ahead of economic reality.

Investors would do well to remember what happened during the dot.com boom.

In the late 1990s, investors poured money into internet companies on the assumption that the new technology would transform commerce and communication.

While they were right about the internet’s potential, many were wrong about the companies they backed and the prices they paid.

The lesson was that investors could correctly anticipate a technological revolution and still lose fortunes betting on it.

The cryptocurrency boom and bust offers another warning.

Cryptocurrencies attracted investors with promises of decentralised finance, better financial infrastructure and attractive returns. But soaring crypto prices also encouraged speculation, excessive leverage and a culture of hype and excess.

The collapse of the TerraUSD stablecoin and its sister token Luna in May 2022 triggered heavy losses and exposed vulnerabilities across the sector.

The crisis deepened in November that year with the implosion of FTX, once one of the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchanges. Founder Sam Bankman-Fried was subsequently convicted of fraud and sentenced to 25 years in prison.

The crypto collapse showed that investor enthusiasm can easily obscure fundamental questions about viability, governance, transparency and risk.

While AI is already generating substantial commercial revenue and delivering practical benefits across industries, the danger is the formation of another speculative bubble.

When expectations eventually disappoint, a sharp market correction could erode confidence across the sector, including companies with sound business models and promising technologies. The result could be a setback for innovation and development of AI, even if the technology’s underlying potential remains intact.

Anthropic’s investors, therefore, face the difficult task of putting a price on a technology that promises benefits, even as its developers acknowledge costs and risks that are difficult to predict and quantify.

What is clear is that greater scrutiny following a Democratic sweep in the US midterms would put pressure on AI companies to exercise financial discipline, rein in excessive spending and demonstrate that their products can generate sustainable profits.

It could encourage investors to pay closer attention to safety and corporate governance, particularly when failures could have far-reaching consequences for society and shareholders.

Nvidia offers a stark reminder of why governance matters.

The chipmaker, whose market value grew more than tenfold from the end of 2022 to its peak in October 2026, became the poster child of the AI boom under co-founder Jensen Huang.

But Huang’s abrupt resignation in November exposed the risks of a company so closely identified with one individual, particularly when it had no publicly known successor ready to take over.

Nvidia has lost about US$1.8 trillion in market value since its October peak, weighed down by concerns over AI valuations compounded by uncertainty over its leadership and future direction.

Its predicament shows that even a company with strong earnings and a commanding market position can suffer when investors begin questioning its governance.

AI may well change the world for the better. But that does not mean investors should pay any price for a stake in its future.
